title: Was he the originator of Chicago dixieland?
summary: He declines the title and credits others.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Oh this is really just a marvellous tribute to you. Now there's something on the inside of this and I don't know where it comes from. But it says that Jimmy McPartland is the originator of
the Chicago variant of dixieland which was evolved in the middle twenties by those musicians who are remembered as the Austin Highschool Gang.
Now would you say that that is true?
That I was what did you say?
That you were the originator of the Chicago variant of dixieland.
Well not the originator. I think we all were. I wouldn't put myself in that category of being the originator. I would say that ....
Because things like that tend to evolve.

I was one of them. Benny Goodman's another and Muggsy Spanier and Frank Ieschemachler (Deschman??) and Bud Freeman. These guys were all stylists on their instruments and we had our influences. And for instance, Muggsy Spanier he loved Louis and you could hear Louis through all his playing. Although he wasn't copying any of Louis' licks. It's the same thing with me and Bix, when Bix said to me I like you kid, you sound like me but you don't copy me. It's the same thing with Louis. I mean, like Muggsy Spanier
he sounded like Louis but he didn't copy him. He played his own way but he did have, his influence was there. And what greater influence could a person have? In my opinion. Musically.

Because I tend to be distrustful of statements like that. I know in literary criticism people get carried away and this one is the best and this one started that. But these things just don't start up with one person.
